title: VPS6 Salary: How to Convert Your Hourly Rate to Annual Pay
description: Learn how to convert a VPS6 salary or any hourly rate to annual, fortnightly, and weekly pay. Includes tax, super, and minimum wage comparisons.
salarySummary: For a VPS6 salary, divide the annual figure by 52 weeks and 38 hours to find the hourly rate; the national minimum wage is $26.44 per hour from 1 July 2026.

faqs.q: How do I convert a VPS6 salary to an hourly rate?
faqs.a: Divide the annual salary by 52 weeks, then divide by 38 hours (the standard full-time week). For example, a $130,000 VPS6 salary gives an hourly rate of about $65.79. This assumes no overtime or allowances.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the national minimum wage and award rates?
faqs.a: The national minimum wage ($26.44/hr from 1 July 2026) is the base for award-free employees. Most workers are covered by a modern award, which sets higher minimum rates for specific industries and roles. Award rates also include penalty rates, allowances, and casual loadings.

faqs.q: How is super calculated on top of my salary?
faqs.a: Super guarantee is 12% of your ordinary time earnings, paid by your employer on top of your salary. For a VPS6 salary of $130,000, that's an extra $15,600 per year, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830.

bodyMarkdown:
## Understanding the VPS6 Salary and Hourly Conversion

If you're looking at a **VPS6 salary** – a classification in the Victorian Public Service – you might want to know what that means per hour, per fortnight, or after tax. The same conversion method works for any hourly rate or annual offer. This guide explains the formula, the key differences between minimum wages and award rates, and how tax and super affect your take-home pay.

### The Basic Formula: Hourly to Annual

Annual gross pay = hourly rate × hours per week × 52 weeks.

For full-time work, the standard week is 38 hours. So if you earn $50 per hour:

$50 × 38 × 52 = $98,800 per year.

To go the other way – say you're offered a **VPS6 salary** of $130,000 – divide by 52 weeks, then by 38 hours:

$130,000 ÷ 52 ÷ 38 = $65.79 per hour.

This assumes you work the same hours every week with no unpaid overtime, penalty rates, or allowances. For a fortnightly figure, multiply the weekly amount by 2. Using the $50/hour example: weekly = $1,900, fortnightly = $3,800.

### National Minimum Wage vs Award Rates vs Enterprise Agreements

The Fair Work Commission sets the **national minimum wage** – from 1 July 2026 it's $26.44 per hour, or $1,004.90 for a 38-hour week. Casual employees get a 25% loading on top, making it $33.05 per hour.

Most employees are covered by a modern award, which sets higher minimum rates for their industry. For example, the Social, Community, Home Care and Disability Services Industry Award has specific classifications with rates above the minimum. You can find the latest pay guides on the [pay guides](/blog) page.

A **VPS6 salary** is not set by a federal award – it comes from the Victorian Public Service Enterprise Agreement. These agreements often provide higher pay and conditions than awards. Always check your specific employment contract or enterprise agreement for your exact rate.

### Tax and Medicare Levy

For the 2026–27 financial year, resident tax rates are:

- $0 – $18,200: nil
- $18,201 – $45,000: 15%
- $45,001 – $135,000: 30%
- $135,001 – $190,000: 37%
- Over $190,000: 45%

Plus the Medicare levy of 2% (with reductions for low-income earners).

Using the $98,800 annual example, the tax would be approximately:

- First $18,200: $0
- Next $26,800 (to $45,000): $4,020
- Remaining $53,800 (to $98,800): $16,140
- Total tax: $20,160
- Medicare: $1,976
- Net after tax and Medicare: about $76,664 per year.

For a **VPS6 salary** of $130,000, you'd be in the 37% bracket on the portion above $135,000. Use the [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) calculator for a personalised estimate.

### Super Guarantee: Paid on Top

Your employer must pay super guarantee of 12% of your ordinary time earnings, on top of your salary. It does not come out of your pay. For a $98,800 salary, that's an extra $11,856 per year in super, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830.

Super is not included in the hourly-to-annual conversion – it's additional. If you're comparing a **VPS6 salary** with a contract rate, remember that contractors often need to arrange their own super.

### Casual Loading and Ordinary-Time Earnings

If you're a casual employee, your hourly rate typically includes a 25% loading. The Fair Work Ombudsman's pay guides show the base rate and the casual rate separately. When converting a casual hourly rate to annual, use the base rate (without loading) for the formula, or note that the annual figure will be higher if you include the loading.

Ordinary-time earnings are what you earn for standard hours – not overtime, penalties, or allowances. The Australian Bureau of Statistics reports average weekly ordinary-time earnings for full-time adults at $2,083.70 per week (May 2026), which annualises to about $108,352. A **VPS6 salary** is typically above this average.

### Using the Timesheet Tool

Our [the timesheet](/) tool lets you enter your base hourly rate and optionally add 25% casual loading. It calculates annual, fortnightly, weekly, and hourly figures, plus estimated tax and super. Remember: the annual figure is an estimate based on 38 hours per week, 52 weeks per year.

### Important Disclaimer

Annual pay here is hourly rate × hours per week × 52. It assumes the same rate every week, no unpaid overtime, no penalty rates, no allowances, and no salary sacrifice. Super is estimated at 12% of ordinary earnings only, paid on top, and stops at the $270,830 maximum contribution base. Tax is the 2026–27 resident scale with the full tax-free threshold. Medicare uses the 2025–26 single reduction thresholds because the 2026–27 reduction thresholds were not confirmed here. HELP, the Medicare levy surcharge, and salary packaging are not deducted. This is an estimate, not a determination of your pay or tax.

For more details on minimum wages and award classifications, see the [minimum wage](/topics/minimum-wage) page. For super and salary packaging information, visit [super and packaging](/topics/super-and-packaging).
